title: Thanksgiving Travel Nightmare: Dual Coastal Storms and Record Tides Threaten Millions
snippet: Millions of holiday travelers face severe flight delays and hazardous roads as strong storms hit both coasts, while San Francisco braces for historic king tides.
content:
Millions of Americans preparing for Thanksgiving travel are bracing for a chaotic week ahead, as major storm systems on both coasts threaten to snarl flights and flood highways during one of the busiest holiday travel periods of the year.

According to AAA projections, a record-breaking 81.5 million people plan to travel at least 50 miles from home between Tuesday and next Monday. But forecasters warn that a double punch of severe weather—fueled by an atmospheric river in the West and a developing nor'easter in the East—could trigger cascading delays across the nation's transportation networks.

Atmospheric River and Historic Tides Batter the West

In the West, an atmospheric river is pushing strong Pacific storms into Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. Heavy downpours, high winds, and hazardous mountain snow are expected to cause significant travel disruptions along Interstate 5 and key mountain passes like Interstate 80 in the Sierra Nevada. Major airport hubs in San Francisco and Seattle are already on alert for weather-related ground stops.

Adding to the chaos in Northern California, the incoming rain coincides with potentially record-breaking king tides—the highest tides of the year. The National Weather Service has issued coastal flood and high surf warnings for the San Francisco Bay Area, rating the shoreline flood risk as extreme on Tuesday and Wednesday. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie warned residents that the city is preparing for unprecedented water levels, urging locals and travelers alike to exercise extreme caution.

East Coast Braces for Nor'easter and Parade Disruptions

Meanwhile, travelers on the East Coast face their own set of headaches. A developing storm system in the Southeast is expected to bring heavy rain and gusty winds to major airport hubs like Atlanta, Charlotte, Orlando, and Miami starting Wednesday. From there, meteorologists project the storm will intensify into a nor'easter as it treks up the Eastern Seaboard on Thanksgiving Day, bringing torrential rain and coastal flooding to the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast.

The storm's powerful winds could prove particularly troublesome for New York City's iconic 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. City guidelines dictate that the parade's massive character balloons cannot fly if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts top 34 mph. Heavy rain and gusty conditions could also delay thousands of flights on Thursday at major hubs in New York, Boston, and Philadelphia.

Airports Under Pressure

The impending weather comes at an already fragile moment for U.S. air travel. The recent tech outage that temporarily grounded Delta Air Lines flights marked the third major systemic disruption in just over a week, leaving travelers on edge even before the first raindrops fell.

With high travel volumes expected to continue through Sunday's return peak, forecasters strongly advise passengers to monitor flight statuses closely and leave extra travel time regardless of whether they are flying or hitting the open road.
